tasks.q: What happens when RAM becomes full?
a: Data that isn't being used right now is moved to secondary storage to free up space
The computer switches off
The CPU slows its clock
Files are deleted permanently
tasks.fb: That borrowed space is called virtual memory.

tasks.q: Which is most likely to fill RAM?
a: Having many large programs open at once
Having a large hard drive
Having a fast CPU
Having a big monitor
tasks.fb: Each program needs its own space in memory.

a: Space on secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full
Memory that only exists in the cloud
A faster type of RAM
The memory used by virtual reality
tasks.fb: It's real storage space, used as if it were memory.

tasks.q: Can the CPU work directly on data held in virtual memory?
a: No: it must be copied back into RAM first
Yes, just as quickly as RAM
Yes, but only for small files
Only when the computer is idle
tasks.fb: That copying back and forth is what costs time.

tasks.q: Put the steps in order for when the CPU needs data that is in virtual memory.
steps: The CPU asks for data that isn't in RAM
Something not currently needed is moved from RAM to the disk
The data is copied from the disk into the free space in RAM
The CPU can now use the data
tasks.fb: Each of these steps involves slow disk access.

tasks.q: Why is virtual memory slower than RAM?
a: Secondary storage takes far longer to read and write than RAM
It uses a different power supply
It is stored in the cloud
The CPU ignores it
tasks.fb: Even a fast SSD is much slower than RAM.

a: The computer spending most of its time swapping data instead of doing useful work
A hard disk being physically damaged
Deleting temporary files
Defragmenting the disk
tasks.fb: It's the point where virtual memory stops helping.

tasks.q: What is the best way to avoid heavy use of virtual memory?
a: Install more RAM
Buy a bigger monitor
Use a faster internet connection
Delete the operating system

tasks.q: Why does doubling RAM make a heavily loaded computer much faster?
a: Far less swapping is needed, so the CPU waits for the disk much less often
The CPU's clock speed doubles
The hard disk spins twice as fast
Programs become smaller
tasks.fb: The time saved is disk time, not CPU time.

tasks.q: The user switches back to the swapped-out word processor. What happens?
a: It is copied back into RAM, and something else is swapped out
It reopens from scratch, losing the work
It runs from the disk at full speed
Nothing: it was never moved
tasks.fb: That's why switching back takes a moment.

tasks.q: Which would remove the delay completely?
a: Having enough RAM to hold all three programs at once
Turning off the monitor
Using a smaller mouse pointer
Closing the ROM
tasks.fb: With enough RAM, no swapping is needed.

tasks.q: Is each statement about virtual memory true or false?
items: It uses secondary storage as extra memory
The CPU can work on it directly, without using RAM
It is slower than using RAM
It is needed because RAM is limited
Adding more RAM reduces how much it is used
It makes a computer faster than having enough RAM
tasks.fb: Virtual memory is a rescue, not an upgrade.

info.title: Page file
info.text: On Windows this space is called the page file; on Linux it's the swap partition. You can see it using up disk space.

info.title: How big?
info.text: Virtual memory is often set to around the same size as the installed RAM, but the operating system usually manages it automatically.

info.title: Thrashing sounds
info.text: On old computers with spinning hard disks, you could hear thrashing: the drive clicking constantly while nothing happened on screen.

info.title: Phones too
info.text: Some phones now use storage as extra RAM in the same way, advertised as 'RAM expansion' or 'virtual RAM'.

info.title: Pages
info.text: Memory is swapped in fixed-size blocks called pages, usually 4 kB, rather than whole programs at a time.

info.title: SSD wear
info.text: Heavy swapping writes a lot of data, which slowly wears out an SSD. Another reason to fit enough RAM.
